prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, and its realisation at fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep the optical lattice clock (B057) to Katori and Ye as my single-part configuration; my position has not changed since round 1. After the full exchange the case still rests on the physics. The magic-wavelength condition is one bounded idea that removes light-shift and motional errors for many neutral atoms at once. It has been reproduced independently at the 10^-18 level, and the result is not disputed. The round-1 files show that the overlap with the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 single-quantum-system prize is the main reservation, and every supporter lists it. I think it is answerable if the citation names neutral-atom lattice trapping and the resulting accuracy and stability, and does not say optical clocks or frequency standards generally. The two-name credit is clean: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the strontium lattice clock to record accuracy and stability. I treat the seven-of-eight support as a cross-check only. What persuades me is that this is the one candidate where the discovery-versus-refinement question, the attribution question and the maturity question can each be answered without a large concession.
statement.case_against: The objection I take most seriously is that this may read as a superb refinement of precision metrology, not a new phenomenon, coming after 2005 and 2012. I do not think that is fatal, because neither earlier prize delivered the many-atom lattice architecture, but a citation that is loose would justify the objection. A second concern is that Lemonde, Bloom, Ludlow, Takamoto and the ion-clock programmes are outside the credit, and Ido and Kimble earlier proposed trapping ideas. I accept this as a real limit on a two-name prize, but it applies to most candidates here and does not call for a third name without a specific documented contribution. Third, the second has not yet been redefined. I would not make the prize wait for it, but the citation must rest on the demonstrated measurement capability and not on that outcome. Lastly, two AMO-adjacent members on this committee may share a lens that overvalues measurement, so the case should hold up against colleagues in condensed matter and elsewhere.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers topological insulators (B053) to Kane, Mele and Molenkamp as a new organising principle with a mature, widely confirmed field, while accepting B057 as a good outcome, and says the difference is framing and weight.
responses.response: I agree that B053 is scientifically very strong and I keep it as my first alternative. A topological invariant that classifies band insulators is a deeper conceptual step than a record in measurement. I still do not move it ahead of B057 because of the attribution. Any three-name set leaves out essential contributors: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for HgTe, Fu for the three-dimensional case, and Hasan or others for the ARPES confirmation. The 2016 prize on topological phases also sits close. The lattice clock needs no such judgement about who is left out. If the committee cannot write a B057 citation that separates it from 2005 and 2012, then your argument becomes the stronger one, and I would back B053 with the Kane, Mele and Molenkamp core, with the Hasan versus Mele choice as the open question. I do not think we are at that point.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the redefinition of the second is a later metrological decision and not a precondition, that the lattice concept is distinct from ion clocks, and he flags his stay in John Hall's laboratory for the chair to judge.
responses.response: On timing I now agree with you more than in round 1. The achievement is complete, since independent clocks agree at 10^-18, and I would not make the prize wait for the redefinition. The citation should still be framed on the demonstrated measurement and not on the redefinition. On the chair's recusal question, a stay in Hall's laboratory is a documented tie to the earlier 2005 work and not to Katori or Ye. Your judgement of the overlap is the one I most want to hear, and you are the one best placed to say where the comb prize ends and the lattice clock begins. I would not require recusal. I would ask you to say plainly whether you think that boundary is sharp enough to write down.

responses.point: Olsson says the lattice clock may be a superb refinement of precision metrology and not a new window on nature, that ion clocks are partly absorbed by the 2012 prize, and that the citation must name the lattice clock specifically.
responses.response: I agree with the narrowing you ask for and I think it settles most of the ion-clock worry. A citation naming magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms in a lattice claims neither the ion work nor the comb. It also answers the refinement argument: the lattice architecture gives a different stability mechanism, with many atoms interrogated in parallel. That is not single-ion control made better. I take your caution that a refinement can still be a refinement, and I do not claim it is a new window on nature. Its case is a measurement capability that is used for tests of constants and relativistic geodesy. On your note about a Chalmers connection, I agree it is not a conflict for B057: I have no recorded tie to Katori, Ye or their groups.

responses.point: Mehlig accepts the merits of B057 but notes the committee would need to say what is new beyond 2005 and 2012, and that Ido and Kimble earlier proposed trapping ideas, which supports his view that the overlap line is not sharp.
responses.response: I think your Ido and Kimble point is correct and should shape the citation. Their earlier ideas show that the concept had precedents, so I would not write the citation as the first idea of trapping atoms for clocks. The step to credit is the demonstration that the magic condition works and the development of the clock to 10^-18 accuracy and stability. That sits with Katori's realisation and Ye's accuracy and stability work and is what independent laboratories reproduced. I would keep that wording and not widen the credit, because the idea having precedents does not change who demonstrated the clock performance.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can write a B057 citation that separates neutral-atom lattice clocks from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single quantum systems without leaving the part-credit of Ido, Kimble and the other lattice-clock groups unsaid.
Whether Ye's contribution, which is partly many-body clock physics and comb-linked comparison, is the part most exposed to the earlier prizes, and whether the citation can still describe it fairly.
How the committee should treat the redefinition of the second. I treat it as neither a condition nor irrelevant: not a precondition, but not a basis for the citation either.
If B053 is needed, whether a Kane, Mele and Molenkamp credit is defensible against Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan and against the 2016 prize.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I opened with circuit QED (B021) at rank 1. As director of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and a professor at Chalmers working on circuit and waveguide QED, I have a professional interest in B021, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in that field. I would recuse myself or discount my judgement on B021 and related superconducting-circuit candidates, and that is why I have not put it forward as my preferred part; it is only listed as an alternative. I have no recorded personal or institutional connection to Katori, Ye or the lattice-clock groups, and no connection to the B053 candidates. Eva Olsson has noted that I am a Chalmers colleague, which does not bear on B057.
